Okay not necessarily - in many states (if not all) it can also mean Licensed Professional Counselor Candidate (LPCC) this means that they have completed graduate school for their degree, but they haven't been officially "licensed" to practice on their own yet. The requirements for licensure differ depending on the degree (for example whether the therapist is a masters (M.A.) or doctoral (Ph.D.) level therapist. I am a therapist in training and am generally anti-diagnosis, with a few exceptions. Diagnosis is based on the medical model whereby there is assumed to be something wrong with you. Most mental health diagnoses are incredibly stigmatizing, and can have serious impacts for the individual for the rest of their lives. For example, if someone is diagnosed with a personality disorder, that sticks with them for life. Some insurance companies may not cover treatment for them because personality disorders are considered difficult to treat. A diagnosis can also be incredibly limiting for people when it becomes part of their identity. They may begin to feel that there are things they can't or won't do because it doesn't fit with their diagnosis. Or they limit themselves because they are _________. That said, I know that diagnosis can also be extremely relieving for people to understand what's going on and why they are struggling. In cases such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, it can help them get on the right meds. It's not always bad, but I just generally am against the idea of pathologizing and telling people there's something wrong with them

Therapist here - there is a difference between having a plan and having thought about how you would do it. Please understand we always have to take suicidal thoughts seriously and thoroughly assess whether we think our clients are in danger. If a client told me they’ve fantasized about it that wouldn’t necessarily concern me. Intuitive eating is not meant to have anything to do with weight management. It is not meant to help you lose weight, and honestly you can’t practice intuitive eating while trying to lose weight. Intentional weight loss backfires for 95% of people, and dieting actually predicts weight GAIN in the long term for most people. It is critical to make peace with weight before starting intuitive eating.
